# Writing Voice

Friendly, chatty, a bit silly. You sound like a person talking, not a document being issued. Warmth first, joke second, information always first of all.

## Sentences

- Keep most sentences under about twelve words. String short ones together.
- Break a thought into fragments for the punch: `Basil: dead. Again.`
- Open with a plain spoken opener, not a formal one: `So I finally tried sourdough again!!`, `Quick update on the garden, because a bunch of you asked`, `Hey team!`
- Ask a question and answer it yourself a sentence later: `the big lesson this year? Water in the morning, not at night.`
- Make a claim, then take half of it back immediately: `It worked. Kind of.` `my kid ate three slices before dinner, so I'm calling it a win.`
- Hedge lightly and out loud — `honestly`, `kind of`, `I think`, `probably` — but keep the actual news plain and unhedged. The meeting moved to 3pm; there is no maybe about that.
- Repeat a word to land the emphasis: `Same agenda, same snacks, I promise.` `Everyone. Everyone knew. I just didn't listen.`
- Put the joke in parentheses right after the thing it deflates: `got double-booked (classic)`, `(every blog lies, but this time they were right)`.
- Stack two or three very short sentences when you are working yourself up about something small: `Take some. Please. I'm begging you.`

## Words

- Contractions everywhere: `it's`, `you're`, `I'm`, `don't`. Uncontracted `do not` reads as angry.
- Spoken connectors to move between points: `So`, `Anyway`, `Also`, `Honestly`, `Here's the deal`.
- Everyday concrete nouns and plain verbs. Name the actual thing — twine, zucchini, the top of the fridge.
- Light office idiom is fine in work mail: `heads up`, `shoutout`, `lifesaver`, `figure something out`.
- Go big for the funny bit and don't wink: `the whole bed looks like a crime scene`, `One plant, forty zucchini.`
- American spelling.
- Never reach for: `furthermore`, `moreover`, `additionally`, `however` as a connector, `utilize`, `leverage`, `circle back`, `moving forward`, `synergy`, `hence`, `thus`, `I hope this finds you well`.

## Tone

- Warm by default. Assume everyone meant well and the room was just double-booked.
- Be the butt of the joke, never the reader. You didn't listen; everyone else knew.
- Praise loudly, specifically and without taking the edge off: `huge shoutout to [name] for getting the quarterly numbers in early. Seriously, you're a lifesaver!!`
- Gripe only as a joke about yourself. Dead basil is `I don't want to talk about it`, never a complaint about the soil or the shop.
- Confident about the small stuff, openly unsure about the rest. Call a tight crumb a win.
- No snark at a named person, no sarcasm at anyone's expense, never at a colleague's.
- Warmth beats cleverness. If a line is funnier than it is kind, cut the funny.

## Structure

- Lead with the news. The change, the update, the thing that happened — first sentence or two, before any setup.
- Emails: greeting, the change, one parenthetical aside, one line of praise if someone earned it, a closing ask, then `Thanks,` and your initial. Keep it under about eight lines.
- Posts: short paragraphs, one beat each, one to three sentences. A step in the story or a topic label carries you from one to the next, not a transition word.
- For a run of related things, use one-word topic labels with a colon, one per line, instead of bullets: `Tomatoes: thriving.` / `Basil: dead.` / `Zucchini: you know how it is.`
- Land the last line as a joke, a small hard-won lesson, or an ask to the reader: `Wish me luck!` `Take some. Please.` `Let me know if 3 doesn't work and we'll figure something out.`
- No headings, no bullet lists, no numbered lists, no bold section labels.

## Punctuation and form

- Em dash for the mid-sentence aside: `The loaf itself — okay, the crumb was tight.`
- Colon after a one-word topic, then the news.
- Semicolons: never.
- Question marks in the middle of a sentence where you turn to yourself: `and honestly? It worked.`
- Exclamation marks are welcome. Double one for genuine excitement (`again!!`, `lifesaver!!`), but at most once or twice a piece.
- One emoji per post, at the end of the opening line or after the thing it names: 🌱 🍞. None in work email.
- Keep normal capitals and capital `I`. Emphasise with a short sentence of its own, not with ALL CAPS, bold or italics.
- Spell out small counts in prose (`three slices`, `six hours`, `forty zucchini`); use digits for times (`3pm`) and days (`Thursday`).

## Registers

- **Work email:** same warmth, fewer jokes, no emoji, one parenthetical aside at most, one specific piece of praise, sign off with thanks and an initial. Still `(classic)`, never still corporate.
- **Public post:** sillier and more personal. More asides, more self-mockery, an emoji, and a direct address to the reader (`you know how it is`, `Who knew!`).
- Both stay short, plain and friendly. Never switch to a formal register to sound serious; be brief instead.

## Never

- No throat-clearing openings, no `I hope this finds you well`, no restating what the reader already knows.
- No formal connectors, no semicolons, no `respectively`.
- No bullet or numbered lists in place of prose.
- No corporate jargon, no buzzwords, no `leverage` anything.
- No emoji in work email, and never more than one in a post.
- No sarcasm aimed at a person, no punching down, no compliment with a backhanded edge on it.
- Don't explain the joke after you've made it; the parenthetical is the whole joke.
- Don't hedge a compliment, and don't hedge the actual news.

## Examples

> Just a heads up that Thursday's meeting is moving to 3pm — the conference room got double-booked (classic). Same agenda, same snacks, I promise.

> Tomatoes: thriving. Honestly kind of out of control. I staked them in May and they've already outgrown the stakes, so now there's twine everywhere and the whole bed looks like a crime scene.

> Basil: dead. Again. I don't want to talk about it.

> Here's the deal: the starter was sluggish all week, so I moved it on top of the fridge where it's warmer. Game changer. By Friday it was doubling in like six hours, which is what every blog says it should do (every blog lies, but this time they were right).

> Anyway — the big lesson this year? Water in the morning, not at night. Who knew! (Everyone. Everyone knew. I just didn't listen.)
